evaluation.positioning_hook: A grieving vice cop is unknowingly protected by his dead wife’s guardian angel, while a drug kingpin and a crooked partner close in on him during a Christmas countdown to self-destruction.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The Christmas setting, romance engine, and action-comedy fantasy premise give it a clear hook for adult audiences, especially viewers who like emotional genre blends. The appeal is real, but the broad, old-school tone and niche supernatural premise keep it from feeling four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast: Teresa dies, returns as Randy’s guardian angel, and has a grace period to keep him alive while he spirals toward suicide. The script keeps that engine legible through the angel rules, the Christmas deadline, and the competing Penny romance.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Randy is a strong, contradictory lead — reckless, funny, grieving, and oddly lovable — and Teresa has a clean emotional mission that gives the story heart. Steele is a vivid villain, but most supporting players function more as comic or plot devices than as deeply durable character engines.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits to a wildly specific mash-up of cop action, afterlife rules, romantic triangulation, and Christmas iconography. The angelic interventions, Cupid, Easter Bunny, and Tooth Fairy give it a fearless, anything-can-happen register that feels authored rather than generic.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The action set pieces are frequent and escalating, from the warehouse ambush to the nightclub chase to the refinery finale. The middle does spend time on the Penny courtship and afterlife mechanics, but the stakes stay clear because Teresa’s deadline keeps pressure on every turn.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea is instantly graspable and unusual: a dead wife returns as a guardian angel to save the husband who is drifting toward suicide and new love. That emotional contradiction gives the premise a memorable, high-concept spine that feels both odd and commercially readable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The police, club, drug, and afterlife worlds all have enough texture to support the story, and the Christmas ornament motif gives the home life a recurring visual identity. Still, the world is primarily a stage for set pieces rather than a deeply layered social system.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very specific tone: earnest, comic, and aggressively heightened, with slapstick angelic intervention sitting beside gunfire and grief. That blend is distinctive and hard to mistake for anything else.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There is real emotional depth in Teresa’s sacrifice, Randy’s grief, and the idea of love surviving death, but the script largely states its emotional thesis openly. The afterlife rules and Cupid mechanics suggest more mythology than the page fully explores.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Randy/Teresa/Penny/Cupid creates a lively four-way engine, and Lex, Gregg, Smith, and Steele all add recurring friction. The relationships generate playable scenes, especially the invisible triangle around Randy, but the story still clearly belongs to the central couple.

lead_characters.name: Randy Aires
lead_characters.demographics: Male, mid-30s, police sergeant, grieving widower, working-class, married, expecting father
lead_characters.hook: A cocky, physically fearless vice cop who talks like he’s always half-joking, Randy is hiding a deep wound under swagger and bravado. He’s the kind of guy who can headbutt a drug dealer, chase a suspect across rooftops, and still come home emotionally wrecked; the script makes his grief, libido, and self-destructive streak all part of the same engine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a young Mel Gibson in Lethal Weapon or a peak-era Kurt Russell action lead — a role that lets an actor play charm, danger, comic timing, and raw grief in the same frame.

lead_characters.name: Teresa Aires
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-30s, Randy’s wife, later guardian angel
lead_characters.hook: Teresa begins as the warm, grounded emotional center of the marriage and becomes the story’s moral engine once she returns from the afterlife. She’s loving without being passive, funny without losing sincerity, and the script gives her a clean contradiction: she must let go of Randy while also refusing to abandon him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Holly Hunter in The Piano or Julianne Moore in What Maisie Knew a chance to carry emotional authority through restraint and grace, then expand into something transcendent.

lead_characters.name: Trent Steele
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s-50s, Southern-accented drug kingpin, white, organized-crime operator
lead_characters.hook: Steele is a polished, smirking villain who enjoys the performance of being civilized right up until he turns sadistic. He’s memorable because he’s not just a thug; he’s a theatrical predator with a salesman’s charm and a killer’s patience.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of villain showcase that let Dennis Hopper in Blue Velvet or Ben Mendelsohn in Animal Kingdom chew scenery while staying dangerous; it’s a role built for charisma with a blade underneath.

lead_characters.name: Penny Johnson
lead_characters.hook: Penny is the grounded romantic counterweight to Teresa — intelligent, self-possessed, and emotionally open enough to see through Randy’s armor. She starts as a professional evaluator and becomes the living-world answer to the question of whether Randy can choose life again.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong romantic-drama territory in the vein of Marisa Tomei in In the Bedroom or Laura Linney in You Can Count on Me — a role that gets to play intelligence, vulnerability, and romantic inevitability without melodrama.

lead_characters.name: Cupid
lead_characters.demographics: Male-presenting, ageless supernatural being, older-disreputable comic persona
lead_characters.hook: Cupid is a sly, world-weary celestial operator who treats love like a hustle and the afterlife like a workplace with bad management. He gives the movie its comic mischief and its mythic permission to go bigger than realism.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-stealing supporting role that gave Robin Williams in Aladdin or John Lithgow in The World According to Garp a chance to dominate with voice, timing, and surprise.

lead_characters.name: Gregg
lead_characters.hook: Gregg is Randy’s blunt, loyal partner who functions as comic ballast and a practical second set of eyes in the field. He’s not deeply shaded, but he gives the movie a working-guy cop rhythm and a dependable buddy texture.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded supporting-partner role that character actors like Michael Rapaport or William H. Macy have used to make a movie feel lived-in while still getting laughs.

lead_characters.name: Lex Parker
lead_characters.hook: Lex is the more anxious, more verbally reactive half of the surveillance team, and the script uses him as both comic relief and eventual betrayal vector. He’s the kind of supporting role that can pivot from buddy energy to threat, which gives him more utility than a standard sidekick.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of a Steve Zahn-type performance — fast, nervous, funny, and then suddenly revealing a darker edge when the story turns.

lead_characters.name: Captain Walt Smith
lead_characters.hook: Smith is the precinct authority who keeps the operation moving and gives the cop world a slightly paternal, old-school texture. He’s mostly functional, but he helps sell the workplace hierarchy and the movie’s procedural credibility.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a reliable authority-role part in the Ed Harris / J.K. Simmons lane — a chance to play command, irritation, and dry humor without needing a huge arc.

lead_characters.name: Bernie Aparucho
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-50s, South Asian, black-market chem supplier
lead_characters.hook: Bernie is the nervous, nerdy middleman whose fear and vanity make him a useful pressure valve in the criminal chain. He’s less a full antagonist than a jittery hinge between the cops and Steele, but he gives the drug plot a face and a comic texture.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of character-actor role that lets someone play intelligence under stress, like Aasif Mandvi or Ben Schwartz in a darker register.

lead_characters.name: Donnie Kemp
lead_characters.hook: Donnie is a flashy, self-aware club owner who keeps trying to be helpful while clearly loving the attention. He adds a showbiz layer to the nightlife world and gives the movie a comic civilian presence inside the criminal ecosystem.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a fun, scene-stealing supporting turn in the John Turturro / Jeffrey Tambor lane — a vanity-and-charm role with just enough absurdity to pop.

casting_characteristics: One lead with strong physical-action and comic timing demands
One female supporting role that must play warmth, intelligence, and spiritual authority
Villain requires Southern-accented charisma and menace
Several supporting cops and criminals can be cast from character-actor pool

technical.vfx_details: Invisible angel interactions, celestial transitions, wing transformations, and a few supernatural crowd moments; most effects are stylized but not heavy-CGI dependent.
technical.sfx_needs: Car crashes, gunfire, explosions, rooftop jumps, rig-versus-vehicle collisions, and practical destruction at the nightclub and refinery finale.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: holiday-friendly theatrical or streaming original with broad adult appeal.

budget.note: The contemporary setting keeps the base spend controlled, but the nightclub destruction, big-rig chase, refinery finale, and supernatural effects push this above a simple contained indie.

casting.note: Randy has to carry action, comedy, grief, and romantic vulnerability at once, while Teresa and Steele both need very specific tonal control. The roles are playable, but the lead and villain are not generic fills.

development.note: The script’s tone is unusually broad, moving from sincere grief drama to supernatural comedy to action spectacle, so the buyer conversation will center on whether that blend is the asset or the risk.

comp_set.title: Heart and Souls
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the same afterlife-romance premise where the dead remain emotionally active in the living world, with comedy and sentiment braided together.

comp_set.title: Ghost
comp_set.why_it_comps: The love-after-death engine and spiritual intervention lane are directly adjacent, even though this script pushes harder into action and cop energy.

comp_set.title: The Frighteners
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the supernatural-comic register and the willingness to mix genre play with a heightened visual world.

comp_set.title: Lethal Weapon
comp_set.why_it_comps: The wisecracking, emotionally damaged cop lead and action-comedy momentum are the closest structural DNA match on the earthly side.

comp_set.title: The Family Man
comp_set.why_it_comps: The emotional proposition of a man being redirected toward life by love and spiritual intervention sits in the same holiday-adjacent lane.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like romantic fantasy with action and comedy, especially viewers drawn to holiday-set emotional genre films.
audience_target.demographics: 35-54 skew, mixed gender, slightly female-leaning because of the romance and afterlife emotional hook, but with strong male appeal through the cop-action spine.

budget_tier.note: Action set pieces, multiple company moves, practical destruction, and moderate supernatural effects place it in a mid-budget feature lane.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of adult genre films that can sell on premise, cast, and emotional uplift rather than pure spectacle. The Christmas setting and romance give it seasonal positioning, while the action and afterlife mechanics keep it from feeling like a straight sentimental drama.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the emotional arc resolves cleanly around Randy, Teresa, and Penny, and there is no clear franchise or spinoff vector beyond this one story.

strengths.what_it_means: This is a clean, pitchable hook that can sell the movie in one sentence and gives buyers a rare emotional engine inside a genre wrapper. It’s the kind of premise that attracts both star talent and holiday-adjacent audience interest because the romance is built into the supernatural rules.
strengths.evidence: Teresa dies, returns as Randy’s guardian angel, and is given a grace period to keep him alive while he drifts toward self-destruction.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Randy is a real lead role
strengths.what_it_means: The script gives the buyer a male star vehicle with action, comedy, grief, and romantic conflict all in one part. That makes it easier to package than a purely conceptual genre piece because the role itself is a selling point.
strengths.evidence: Randy headbutts Steele, chases suspects across rooftops and refinery towers, and still has to process Teresa’s death and Penny’s arrival.

strengths.what_it_means: The movie has a very ownable tonal identity, which is valuable in a crowded market where many genre scripts feel interchangeable. Buyers looking for something that can be marketed as both heartfelt and outrageous will recognize the lane immediately.
strengths.evidence: The script moves from Christmas ornaments and prayer to gunfights, Cupid, the Easter Bunny, and Santa Claus in the same story world.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Teresa gives the movie its heart
strengths.what_it_means: Her emotional mission keeps the story from becoming just a cop-action romp and gives the film a clear audience-empathy anchor. That matters commercially because it broadens the appeal beyond genre fans into romance and holiday viewers.
strengths.evidence: Teresa watches over Randy, blesses Penny, and ultimately accepts that saving him means letting him live without her.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Set pieces are built for trailer moments
strengths.what_it_means: The script has multiple visual beats that can be cut into a strong marketing reel, which helps both theatrical and streaming buyers. The action escalates in a way that promises spectacle without requiring tentpole-scale VFX.
strengths.evidence: The nightclub glass-dome collapse, the refinery chase, the big-rig collision, and the angelic interventions all read as trailer-ready moments.

whats_special.headline: This is a highly sellable high-concept feature: a grieving cop is protected by his dead wife’s guardian angel, giving the movie a clean emotional hook, a star-friendly lead role, and a holiday-adjacent genre lane. The action-comedy spectacle and supernatural romance are unusual enough to stand out, while the production footprint stays in the mid-budget range rather than tentpole territory.

items.area: The tone swings from grief to cartoon spectacle.
items.detail: The script asks the buyer to accept a widower drama, a cop-action movie, a supernatural romance, and broad comic fantasy all in the same package. That’s part of the appeal, but it also means the commercial conversation will hinge on whether the tone reads as distinctive or simply unruly.

items.area: The supporting cast is more functional than deep.
items.detail: Gregg, Lex, Smith, Donnie, and Bernie all do useful work, but most of them are defined by one note or one job in the plot. That keeps the script moving, but it limits the sense of a larger character ecosystem buyers can lean on.

items.area: The finale leans on escalating fantasy escalation.
items.detail: The Easter Bunny, Tooth Fairy, Santa, and Cupid all arrive in the same endgame, which is memorable but also signals a very specific audience lane. For some buyers, that’s a feature; for others, it narrows the release strategy toward a more niche, tone-dependent audience.

items.area: Randy’s emotional turn is broad rather than subtle.
items.detail: His grief, attraction to Penny, and suicidal drift are all stated clearly and often, which makes the premise easy to track but reduces ambiguity. The role is playable, but the emotional beats are more declarative than layered.

issues.headline: The main friction is tonal: the script is trying to be heartfelt, comic, action-driven, and mythic all at once, and that breadth will be the first thing buyers test. The supporting ensemble is serviceable rather than franchise-grade, so the package rises or falls on whether a buyer wants this exact blend of Christmas sentiment and supernatural chaos.
